d:chapter.d:title: Conic Sections
d:chapter.d:para: In this chapter we will study parabola, ellipse and hyperbola, their properties and elements like tangents and normals. The study of conic sections combines geometry and algebra. Using the coordinate plane, every conic can be represented by an equation in $x$ and $y$, allowing geometric properties to be studied analytically. Conics have rich mathematical structures involving focus, directrix, axis, eccentricity, tangents, normals, and chords.
Pair of straight lines, circles, parabolas, ellipses and hyperbolas are sections of a right circular cone by a plane, and so they are called conic sections.

As you can see in the that when a plane cuts the right circular cone perpendicular to the axis of the cone then we get a circle, when the plane cuts the cone parallel to the generator we get a parabola, when the plane is parallel to the axis we get hyperbola, and when the cone is neither parallel nor perpendicular to axis or generator we get an ellipse.

d:sect1.d:title: Definition
d:sect1.d:para: A conic section is defined as the locus of a point, which moves in a plane such that the ratio of its distance from a fixed point and a fixed line is a constant.

The fixed point is called the focus and the fixed line the directrix of the conic section. The constant ratio is called eccentricity of the curve and is usually denoted by $e$. One such conic section is shown below:

If $e = 1$, then the resulting coninc is a parabola, if $e < 1$, then the resulting conic is an ellipse, and if $e > 1$, then the resulting conic is a hyperbola. In the given diagram $\frac{PS}{PN} = e$.
The straight line perpendicular from the focus to the directrix is called the axis of the conic. The point of intersection of the conic and its axis us called the vertex of the conic.
In the given diagram $S$ is the focus, $AN$ the directrix, $AS$ is the axis and $A$ is the vertex of the conic.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of a Conic
d:sect2.d:para: Let $S(\alpha, \beta)$ be the focus and $QN$ the directrix whose equation is $Ax + By + C = 0$.
Let $P(x, y)$ be any point on the conic section. From $P$ draw $PN \perp QN$. Let $e$ be the eccentricity, then by definition $\frac{PS}{PN} = e \Rightarrow PS^2 = e^2PN^2$.
$PS^2 = (x - \alpha)^2 + (y - \beta)^2$ and $PN^2 = \frac{(Ax + By + C)^2}{A^2 + B^2}$

$\Rightarrow (x - \alpha)^2 + (y - \beta)^2 = \frac{e^2(A x + B y + C)^2}{A^2 + B^2}$, which on simplification will have the form $x^2 + y^2 + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$, where $a, b, c, f, g, h$ are constants.
Corollary: Let the focus $S$ lie on the directrix $QN$ and $S$ be taken as the origin and $QN$ be taken as the $y$-axis. Let $P(x, y)$ be any point on the conic then
$\frac{PS}{PN} = e \Rightarrow \frac{\sqrt{x^2 + y^2}}{|x|} = e \Rightarrow \left(e^2 - 1\right)x^2 = y^2$, which is a pair of straight lines through the focus or the origin.

Corollary: The general equation of the second degree $ax^2 + 2y^2 + 2hxy + 2gx + 2fy + c = 0$ represents a parabols if $h^2 = ab$ and $\Delta \neq 0$, where $\Delta = abc + 2fgh - af^2 - bg^2 - ch^2$ or alternatively a second degree equation represents a parabola if second degree terms form a complete square and $\Delta neq 0$.
The second degree equation will represent an ellipse if $h^2 < ab$. We will see that a circle is a special case of an ellipse.
The second degree equation will represent a hyperbola if $h^2 > ab$ and $\Delta \neq 0$ and a pair of straight lines if $\Delta = 0$.

d:sect1.d:title: Parabola
d:sect1.d:para: A parabola is the locus of a point which moves so that its distance from a fixed point, called the focus, is equal to the distance from a fixed line, called the directrix.
The straight line perpendicular from the focus to the directrix is called the axis of the parabola.
The equation of the parabola can be obtained if its directrix and focus are given.

Let $S$ be the focus and $QM$ the directrix of the parabola. From $S$ draw $SQ$ perpendicular to the directrix. Let $OP$ be the middle point of $QS$. Take $O$ as the origin and $OS$ as the $x$-axis and $OY$ through $O$ perpendicular to $OS$ as the $y$-axis.
Now $S = (a, 0)$ and the equation of $QM$ is $x = -a$. Let $P(x, y)$ be any point on the parabola. Join $PS$ and drop perpendicular $PM$ on $QM$.
Be definition of the parabola $PS = PM \Rightarrow (x - a)^2 + y^2 = |x + a|^2$ \[y^2 = 4a x\label{eq:6.1}\tag{6.1}\]

d:orderedlist.d:listitem: If the point $(x, y)$ lies on the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ then point $(-x, -y)$ will also lie on the parabola. Hence, the parabola is symmatrical about its axis.
The point of intersection of the axis of a parabola and the parabola itself is called the vertex if the parabola.
If the perpendicular drawn from a point $P$ to the axis of the parabola meets the parabola at its symmateric point $P'$ then $PP'$ is called a double oridinate.

The double ordinate which passes through the focus is called the latus recturm of the parabola. The length of latus rectum of $y^2 = 4ax$ is $4a$.
The equation of the latus ractum of the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ is $x = a$.
Joining any two points on a parabola yields a line segment called chord.
If a chord passes through focus of a parabola is called focal chord.
The distance of any point on a parabola from the focus of the parabola is callled focal distance.

d:sect1.d:para: The other parabolas having the same length of latus rectum as that of $y^2 = 4ax$ are $y^2 + 4a x = 0, x^2 = 4ay$ and $x^2 + 4a y = 0$.

d:sect2.d:title: Intersection of a Line and a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Consider a straight line given by the equation $y = mx + c$ and a parabola given by the equation $y^2 = 4ax$.
Solving the equations gives us $(m x + c)^2 = 4a x \Rightarrow m^2x^2 + 2x(m c - 2a) + c^2 = 0$.

The above equation, which is a quadratic equation in $x$ will have two roots. If the roots are real i.e. $(mc - 2a)^2 - m^2c^2 > 0$, then the will cut the parabola at two different points. If $(m c - 2a)^2 - m^2c^2 = 0$, then there will be a repeated root and the line will be a tangent to the parabola and if $(m c - 2a)^2 - m^2c^2 < 0$, then roots will be imaginary and the line will not inttersect with the parabola.
We see that $(m c - 2a)^2 - m^2c^2 = 0$ is the condition for tangency. Thus, \[ c = \frac{a}{m} \tag{6.2}\]
Thus, any line of the form $y = mx + a/m$ will be a tangent to the parabola.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of a Tangent at a Given Point on a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Let the equation of parabola be $y^2 = 4a x$. Let $P = (x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2)$ be any two points on the parabola. The equation of $PQ$ will be given by
Since both the points lie on the parabola, therefore $y_1^2 = 4a x_1$ and $y_2^2 = 4a x_2$
Subtracting these two equations yields $(y_2 + y_1)(y_2 - y_1) = 4a(x_2 - x_1) \Rightarrow \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}(x - x_1) = \frac{4a}{y_2 + y_1}$
Putting this in (1) gives us $y - y_1 = \frac{4a}{x_2 + x_1}(x - x_1)$
Now, when $Q \rightarrow P, x_2 \rightarrow x_1$ and $y_2 \rightarrow y_1$ so the above equation becomes

d:para.m: $y - y_1 = \frac{4a}{2y_1}(x - x_1) \Rightarrow y y_1 = 2a x + y_1^2 - 2a x_1$

d:sect2.d:para: Substituting $y_1^2 = 4a x_1$ we have \[ y y_1 = 2a(x + x_1) \tag{6.3}\]
which is the equation of the required tangent.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of a Normal at a Given Point on a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: We have obtained the equation of the tangent to a parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ at $(x_1, y_1)$ as $yy_1 = 2a(x + x_1) \ldots$ (1), The slope of tangent is $\frac{2a}{y1}$.
The normal will be perpendicular to the tangent, and hence, its slope will be $-\frac{y_1}{2a}$.
Thus equation of normal would be \[y - y_1 = -\frac{y_1}{2a}(x - x_1) \tag{6.4}\]

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of the Normal in terms of its Slope
d:sect2.d:para: The normal to the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ at $(x_1, y_1)$ is $y - y_1 = -\frac{y_1}{2a}(x - x_1)$.
Let $-\frac{y_1}{2a} = m \Rightarrow y_1 = 2am$. Since $y_1^2 = 4a x_1 \Rightarrow 4a^2m^2 = 4ax_1 \Rightarrow x_1 = a m^2$
$\Rightarrow y - (-2a m) = m(x - a m^2) \Rightarrow y = mx - 2am - am^3$, which is the equation of the normal in terms of its slope.
Notes: The equation of the normal obtained is $y = mx - 2am - am^3$. This normal passes through $(x_1, y_1)$. Thus, $a m^3 + (2a - x_1) + m + y_1 = 0$.
This is a cubic equation in $m$, which will have three roots of which at least one will be real because complex roots occur in pair.
Any three points on the parabola, normals at which pass through a common point, are called co-normal points.

d:sect2.d:title: Parametric Equation of the Parabola $y^2 = 4a x$
d:sect2.d:para: The point $P$ whose coordinates are $x = at^2, y = 2at$ lies on the parabola $y^2 = 4a x$, which can be trivially verified by substituting in $y^2 = 4a x$.
This representation in which $x$ and $y$ are represented using a single parameter $t$ is called the parametric equation of the parabola.
The point $(at^2, 2at)$ is also referred to as the point '$t$'.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of a Chord of a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Consider two points $(at_1^2, 2at_1)$ and $(at_2^2, 2at_2)$ on the parabola forming a chord.
The equation will be given by $y - 2at_1 = \frac{2at_2 - 2at_1}{at_2^2 - at_1^2}(x - at_1^2)$
is the equation of the the chord.

If this line passes through the focus i.e. $(a, 0)$ then $2a + 2at_1t_2 = 0 \Rightarrow t_1t_2 = -1$. Thus, if one point is $t$ then the condition for the chord to pass through the focus requires the other point to be $-\frac{1}{t}$.

d:sect2.d:title: Tangent and Normal at any Point $t$
d:sect2.d:para: The tangent to the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ at the point $(at^2, 2at)$ is given by
$y(2at) = 2a(x + a t^2) \Rightarrow ty = x + at^2$.
The normal to the parabola $y^2 = 4ax$ at the point $(at^2, 2at)$ is given by
$y - 2at = -t(x - at^2) \Rightarrow y + t x = 2at + at^3$.

We see that two tangents at $t_1$ and $t_2$ have $(a t_1t_2, a(t_1 + t_2))$ as their point of intersection and the normals at the same points will have $\left(2a + a\left(t_1^2 + t_2^2 + t_1t_2\right), -a t_1t_2(t_1 + t_2)\right)$ as their point of intersection.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of the Chord of a Parabola whose middle point is $(x_1, y_1)$
d:sect2.d:para: Equation of the parabola is $y^2 = 4ax$. Let $AB$ be a chord of the parabola whose middle point is $P(x_1, y_1)$.
Equation of the chord is $y - y_1 = m(x - x_1)$, where $m$ is the slope of $AB$.
Let $A = (x_2, y_2)$ and $B = (x_3, y_3) \Rightarrow y_2^2 = 4a x_2$ and $y_3^2 = 4a x_3$

d:para.m: $\therefore y_2^2- y_3^2 = 4a(x_2 - x_3) \Rightarrow \frac{y_2 - y_3}{x_2 - x_3} = \frac{4a}{y_2 + y_3}$

d:sect2.d:para: But $P$ is mid-point of $AB$, so we can write $y_2 + y_3 = 2y_1$
Thus, equation of the chord is $y - y_1 = \frac{2a}{y_1}(x - x_1) \Rightarrow y y_1 - 2a(x + x_1) = y_1^2 - 4a x_1$.

d:sect2.d:title: Diameter of a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Diameter of a conic is the locus of mid-points of a series of its parallel chords.
Let the parabola be $y^2 = 4a x\ldots$ (1)
Let $AB$ be one of the chords of a series of parallel chords having slope $m$. Let $P(\alpha, \beta)$ be the mid-point of chord $AB$, then equation of $AB$ will be $T = S_1$.
$\Rightarrow y\beta - 2a(x + \alpha) = \beta^2 - 4a\alpha \ldots$ (2)
Slope of this line is $frac{2a}{\beta}$. But slope of the line $AB$ is $m$, therefore $\frac{2a}{\beta} = m \Rightarrow beta = \frac{2a}{m}$.
Hence, locus of $P(\alpha, \beta)$ i.e. equation of diameter is \[ y = \frac{2a}{m} \tag{6.7}\]
Clearly, this line is parallel to the axis of the parabola.

d:sect2.d:title: The Optical Property of a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: The tangent at any point $P$ on a parabola bisects the angle between the focal chord through $P$ and the perpendicular from $P$ on the directrix.
Let the parabola be $y^2 = 4a x \ldots$ (1)
Let $P(at^2, 2at)$ be a point on the parabola and let $PM \perp \text{ directrix}$.
Equation of the tangent to parabola at $P$ is $yt = x + at^2$. Slope of this tangent $PT$ is $\frac{1}{t} \Rightarrow \tan\theta = \frac{1}{t}$
Slope of $PS = \frac{2at}{a\left(t^2 - 1\right)} = \frac{\frac{2}{t}}{1 - \frac{1}{t^2}} = \frac{2\tan\theta}{1 - \tan^2\theta} = \tan2\theta$.
$\Rightarrow \angle PSX = 2\theta \Rightarrow \angle TPS = \angle PSX - \angle PTS = 2\theta - \theta = \theta$.
Hence, $\angle SPT = \angle MPT = \theta$.
Therefore $PT$ bisects $\angle MPS$.
The other property we know from physics is that rays coming from infinity are reflected by parabolas in such a manner that they pass through focus. We will prove that here.
Let $PN$ be normal to $PT$. In $\triangle PTN, \angle TPN = 90^\circ$ and $\angle PTN = \theta$
Since $PR \parallel TN, \therefore \angle RPN = \angle TNP = 90^\circ - \theta$
Also, $\angle SPN = 180^\circ - \angle PSN - \angle SNP = 180^\circ - 2\theta - \left(90^\circ - \theta\right) = 90^\circ - \theta$
$\therefore \angle SPN = \angle RPN$.
Thus, a ray parallel to the axis of parabola after reflection from parabola passes through the focus.

d:sect1.d:title: Ellipse
d:sect1.d:para: An ellipse is the locus of the point, which moves in the plane so that the ratio of its distance from a fixed point, and a fixed line is a constant, which is less than one.
The fixed point is called the focus, the constant ratio is called the eccentricity, and the fixed straight line is known as the directrix of the ellipse.
In the figure above, $S$ is the focus and $MM'$ the directrix. Let $P$ be any point on the ellipse, then $\frac{PS}{PN} = e < 1$.
Thus, we can find the equation of an ellipse when the coordinates of the focus, the equation of the directrix, and the eccentricity are known.

As you can see an ellipse cuts $x$-axis at $(-a, 0)$ and $(a, 0)$, cuts $y$-axis at $(-b, 0)$ and $(b, 0)$. Equation of ellipse does not change when $x$ or $y$ are changed to $-x$ and $-y$, hence, an ellipse is symmetrical about $x$ and $y$ axes.
We have $y = \pm \frac{b}{a} \sqrt{a^2 - x^2} \Rightarrow a^2 - x^2 \geq 0 \Rightarrow -a \leq x \leq a$.
Similarly, $x = \pm \frac{a}{b} \sqrt{b^2 - y^2} \Rightarrow b^2 - x^2 \geq 0 \Rightarrow -b \leq y \leq b$.

If $(x_1, y_1)$ lies on the curve, so does $(-x_1, -y_1)$. But $(x_1, y_1)$ and $(-x_1, -y_1)$ are points on the line through the origin and are equidistant from the origin. Hence, every chord through the origin $C$ is bisected at $C$. The point $C$ is, therefore, callled the center of the ellipse.

d:sect2.d:title: Second focus and second directrix of an ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: Let $P(x, y)$ be a point on the ellipse and let $C$ be its center. Let the equation of the ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$, where $b^2 = a^2\left(1 - e^2\right)\ldots$ (1)
Here $CA = CA' = a$ and $e$ is the eccentricity of the ellipse and the point $S$ and the line $QN$ are the focus and directrix respectively.
Let us take $S'$ and $Q'$ on the $x$-axis on that side of $C$ which is opposite to the side of $S$ such that $CS' = ae$ and $CQ' = \frac{a}{e}\ldots$ (2)
Let $Q;N' \perp CQ', PN' \perp Q'N'$ and $PM \perp CX$.
Since $P = (x, y)\therefore CM = x, PM = y$. Join $P$ and $S$. Clearly, $PN' = MQ'$
Equation (1) may be rewritten as $x^2\left(1 - e^2\right) + y^2 = a^2\left(1 - e^2\right)$

d:para.m: $\Rightarrow x^2 + y^2 + a^2e^2 = a^2 + e^2x^2\Rightarrow (ae + x)^2 + y^2 = e^2\left(\frac{a}{e} + x\right)^2$
$\Rightarrow \left(CS' + CM\right)^2 + PM^2 = e^2\left(CQ' + CM\right)^2\Rightarrow S'M^2 + PM^2 = e^2Q'M^2$

d:sect2.d:para: $\Rightarrow S'P^2 = e^2N'P^2 \Rightarrow \frac{PS'}{PN'} = e$.
Hence, the distance of $P$ from $S' = e\times$ (the distance of $P$ from $Q'N'$). Hence, $S'$ is a focus and $Q'N'$ is a directrix.
Thus, it is clear that the ellipse has a second focus and a second directrix.

Foci: $S$ and $S'$ are the two foci of the ellipse and their coordinates are $(ae, 0)$ annd $(-ae, 0)$ respectively.
Directrices: $QN$ and $Q'N'$ are the two directrices of the ellipse and their equations are $x = \frac{a}{e}$ and $x = -\frac{a}{e}$ respectively.

Axes: The lines $AA'$ and $BB'$ are called the major and minor axes respectively of the ellipse.
$CA = CA' = a$ and $CB = CB' = b$
$\because 0 < e < 1 \therefore 0 < 1 - e^2 < 1\therefore a^2(1 - e^2) < a^2$
Thus, $b^2 < a^2$ i.e. $b < a$.

Ordinate and double ordinates: Let $P$ be a point on the ellipse. From $P$ we draw $PM \perp AA'$. Produce $PM$ to meet the ellipse at $P'$, then $PM$ is called an ordinate and $PMP'$ is called the double ordinate of point $P$.
Latus rectum: $LL'$ and $MM'$ are the latus rectrum of the ellipse. These lines are perpendicular to the major axis $AA'$ through the foci $S$ and $S'$

Length of latus rectum: Let $LL' = 2k$, then $LS = k$ and $L = (ae, k)$. Since $L(ae, k)$ lies on the ellipse
$\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 \therefore \frac{a^2e^2}{a^2} + \frac{k^2}{b^2} = 1\Rightarrow \frac{k^2}{b^2} = 1 - e^2$
$\Rightarrow k^2 = b^2\left(1 - e^2\right) = \frac{b^4}{a^2}\Rightarrow k = \frac{b^2}{a}$.
Hence, lenth of latus rectum $LSL'$ is $\frac{2b^2}{a}$.
Vertices: The points where major axis of the ellipse meets it are called its vertices. In the given figure $A$ and $A'$ are the vertices.
Diameter: A chord of the ellipse passing through the center is called the diameter of the ellipse. All such chords are bisected by the center.
Focal chord: A chord of the ellipse passing through its focus is called a focal chord.

d:sect2.d:title: Position of a Point w.r.t. an Ellipse

d:figure.d:title: Position of a Point w.r.t. an Ellipse

d:sect2.d:para: Let $D(\alpha, \beta)$ be any point. Let $DM$ be perpendicular to $AA'$.
Case I: When $-a < \alpha < 1$ i.e. $DM$ cuts the ellipse in real distinct points.
Let the perpendicular $DM$ cut the ellipse at $R$ and the major axis at $M$.
Let $RM = y_1$ then $R = (\alpha, y_1)$.
Since $R$ lies on the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$,
$\therefore \frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} + \frac{y_1^2}{b^2} = 1 \therefore \frac{y_1^2}{b^2} = 1 - \frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} \ldots$ (2)
Now $D$ lies outside, on or inside the ellipse according as $MD >, =, < MR$ or $MD^2 >, =, < MR^2$
$\Rightarrow \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} >, = < 1 - \frac{\alpha^2}{a^2}\Rightarrow \frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} + \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} - 1 >, =, < 0$.
Case II: When $\alpha\geq a$ or $\alpha\leq -a$.
In this case $\frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} + \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} - 1\geq 1 + \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} - 1 = \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} > 0$ where $\beta \neq 0$

Hence in all cases $(\alpha, \beta)$ is outside the ellipse if $\frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} + \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} > 0$; on the ellipse if $\frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} + \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} = 0$; and inside the ellipse if $\frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} + \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} < 0$.

d:sect2.d:title: Parametric Equation of an Ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: Clearly $x = a\cos\theta$ and $y = b\sin\theta$ satisfy the equation $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^1} = 1$ for all real values of $\theta$.

Hence, these values, where $\theta$ is the parameter is the parametric equation of the ellipse. Hence, coordinates of any point on the ellipse may be taken as $(a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)$. This point is also called point '$\theta$'. This angle $\theta$ is called the eccentric angle of the point $(a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)$ on the ellipse.

d:sect2.d:title: Auxilliary Circle and Geometrical Meaning of the Eccentric Angle of a Point
d:sect2.d:para: Auxilliary Circle: The circle described on the major axis of an ellipse as diameter is called the auxilliary circle of the ellipse.

Let the equation of the ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$, then the equation of the auxilliary circle is $x^2 + y^2 = a^2$. Let $P(a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)$ be a point on the ellipse. Draw $PM\perp AA'$. Let $PM$ cut the auxilliary cirle at $Q$.
Let $\angle QCA = \alpha$ then $Q = (a\cos\alpha, a\sin\alpha)$.
But $x$-coordinate of $Q = x$-coordinate of $P$.
$\therefore a\cos\alpha = a\cos\theta \Rightarrow \alpha = \theta$.
Clearly, $QM:PM = a\sin\alpha : b\sin\theta = a\sin\theta:b\sin\theta = a:b$.

d:sect2.d:title: An Important Property

d:para.d:emphasis: The sum of the focal distances of any point on an ellipse is a constant and is equal to the length of the major axis of the ellipse.

d:sect2.d:para: Let $P(x, y)$ be any point on the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.
Then by definition $SP = ePN, S'P = ePN'\Rightarrow SP + S'P = e\left(PN + PN'\right) = eNN' = eQQ' = e\left(CQ + CQ'\right)$
But $CQ = \frac{a}{e}$ and $CQ' = \frac{a}{e} \therefore SP + S'P = 2a = AA'$, where $AA'$ is the length of the major axis of the ellipse.

d:sect2.d:title: Tangent of an Ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: Let the equation of ellipse by $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1). Also, let $P(x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(x_2, y_2)$ be two points on the ellipse.
Equation of the chord $PQ$ is $y - y_1 = \frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1}(x - x_1)\ldots$ (2)
Since $P$ and $Q$ are on the ellipse, therefore, $\frac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \frac{y_1^2}{b^2} = 1$ and $\frac{x_2^2}{a^2} + \frac{y_2^2}{b^2} = 1$
Subtracting $\frac{y_2 - y_1}{x_2 - x_1} = -\frac{b^2}{a^2}\left(\frac{x_2 + x_1}{y_2 + y_1}\right)$
Putting this in equation (2) gives us $y - y_1 = -\frac{b^2}{a^2}\left(\frac{x_2 + x_1}{y_2 + y_1}\right)(x - x_1)$
Now, when $Q\rightarrow P, x_2 \rightarrow x_1, y_2\rightarrow y_1$, so the above equation becomes
Simplifying gives the equation of tangent as \[\frac{xx_1}{a^2} + \frac{yy_1}{b^2} = 1 \tag{6.9}\]
which is the required equation of the tangent to an ellipse at $P(x_1, y_1)$.

d:sect2.d:title: Normal of an Ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: Let $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ be an ellipse and $P(x_1, y_1)$ be a point on it.
We have derived the equation of tangent at $P$ as $\frac{xx_1}{a^2} + \frac{yy_1}{b^2} = 1$.
The slope of normal at this point is $\frac{a^2}{b^2}\times\frac{y_1}{x_1}$.
Thus, equation of normal is $y - y_1 = \frac{a^2y_1}{b^2x_1(x - x_1)}$ i.e.
Putting $P(a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)$ the equation becomes \[ax\sec\theta - by\csc\theta = a^2 - b^2 \tag{6.11}\]

d:sect2.d:title: Intersection of a Line and an Ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: Let the equation of the line be $y = mx + c$ and that of an ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.
The points of intersection of the line and the ellipse can be obtained by solving the two equations simultaneously.
The abscissae of the point of intersection is given by $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{(mx + c)^2}{b^2} = 1$
i.e. $\left(b^2 + a^2m^2\right)x^2 + 2a^2cmx + a^2\left(c^2 - b^2\right) = 0\ldots$ (1)

Let $x_1, x_2$ be the roots of the quadratic equation (1). The line meets the ellipse in real and distinct points if the roots are real and different. The line is a tangent to the ellipse if $x_1 = x_2$ and the line does not intersect with the ellipse if the roots are complex numbers.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of a Tangent in Terms of Its Slope
d:sect2.d:para: Let the equation of the line be $y = mx + c$ and that of an ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.
We have seen that roots of (1) should be equal for tangency. Thus, discriminant must be zero i.e.

d:para.m: $\Rightarrow b^2\left(-c^2 + b^2 + a^2m^2\right) = 0\Rightarrow c^2 = b^2 + a^2m^2 \Rightarrow c = \pm \sqrt{a^2m^2 + b^2}$

d:sect2.d:para: which is the required condition for tangency. Thus, the equation of the line is $y = mx \pm\sqrt{a^2m^2 + b^2}$, which are tangents to the ellipse for all values of $m$.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of the Chord of an Ellipse Whose Eccentric Angles are $\theta$ and $\phi$
d:sect2.d:para: Let the ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Let $P(a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)$ and $Q(a\cos\phi, b\sin\phi)$ be any two points on ellipse (1).
Equation of chord $PQ$ is $y - b\sin\theta = \frac{b(\sin\theta - \sin\phi)}{a(\cos\theta - \cos\phi)}(x - a\cos\theta)$
Simplifying $\frac{x}{a}\cos\frac{\theta + \phi}{2} + \frac{y}{b}\sin\frac{\theta + \phi}{2} = \cos\frac{\theta - \phi}{2}$
Note: When $\phi\rightarrow \theta$, chord $PQ$ becomes tangent at $P$. Thus, equation of tangent at $P$ is $\frac{x}{a}\cos\theta + \frac{y}{b}\sin\theta = 1$.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of the Chord of an Ellipse, Whose Middle Point is Given
d:sect2.d:para: Let the ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1 \ldots$ (1)
Let $P(x_1, y_1)$ be the the mid-point of a chord $AB$ of the ellipse (1). Let $m$ be the slope of chord $AB$. Then $m = \frac{y_2 - y_3}{x_2 - x_3}\ldots$ (2)
Since $A$ and $B$ are on the ellipse, therefore $\frac{x_2^2}{a^2} + \frac{y_2^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (3) and $\frac{x_3^2}{a^2} + \frac{y_3^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (4)
Subtracting (3) and $(4)$ gives us $\frac{y_2 - y_3}{x_2 - x_3} = -\frac{b^2}{a^2}\frac{x_1}{y_1}$
Now equation of the chord $AB$ is $y - y_1 = -\frac{b^2}{a^2}\frac{x_1}{y_1}(x - x_1)$
$\Rightarrow \frac{xx_1}{a^2} + \frac{yy_1}{b^2} - 1 = \frac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \frac{y_1^2}{b^2} - 1\Rightarrow T = S_1$, where $T$ and $S_1$ have usual meanings.

d:sect2.d:title: Equation of Pair of Tangents to an Ellipse from an External Point
d:sect2.d:para: Let the given ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Let $P(x_1, y_1)$ be an external point.

Let $Q(\alpha, \beta)$ be any point on the chord of the ellipse passing through $P(x_1, y_1)$. Coordinates of any point $R$ on the chord dividing the line segment $PQ$, joining $P(x_1, y_1)$ and $Q(\alpha, \beta)$ in the ratio $\lambda:1$ will be $\left(\frac{\lambda\alpha + x_1}{\lambda + 1}, \frac{\lambda\beta + y_1}{\lambda + 1}\right)$.
If this point $R$ lies on the ellipse (1), then

$\Rightarrow \left(\frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} + \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} - 1\right)\lambda^2 + 2\left(\frac{x_1\alpha}{a^2} + \frac{y_1\beta}{b^2} - 1\right)\lambda + \left(\frac{x_1^2}{a^2} + \frac{y_1^2}{b^2} - 1\right) = 0\ldots$ (2)

(2) is a quadratic equation in $\lambda$. If the chord through $P(x_1, y_1)$ cuts the ellipse in two coincident points i.e. if the two values of $\lambda$ are real and equal then the chord through $P(x_1, y_1)$ will become tangent to the ellipse from $P(x_1, y_1)$.
Thus, for the line $PQ$ to become tangent to the ellipse (1)
Hence, locus of $Q(\alpha, \beta)$ i.e. equation of pair of tangents from $P(x_1, y_1)$ is
This can be written as $SS_1 = T^2$, where $S, S_1$ and $T$ have usual meanings.

d:sect2.d:title: Pole and Polar of an Ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: Let $A$ and $B$ be any two points on the ellipse and a point $P$ is given on this line outside the ellipse. Let the tangents at $A$ and $B$ meet at $Q$.
Locus of $Q$ is called the polar of point $P$ w.r.t. the ellipse.
We will see that polar of a point w.r.t. an ellipse is a straight line.
If line $LM$ is the polar of the point $P$ w.r.t. an ellipse, then point $P$ is called the pole of the line $LM$ w.r.t. the ellipse.
d:sect2.d:sect3:
Equation of Polar of a Point
Let the ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Let $P(x_1, y_1)$ be a given point. Let a line through $P$ cut the ellipse (1) at two points $A$ and $B$. Let $Q(\alpha, \beta)$ be the point of intersection of the tangents to the ellipse at $A$ and $B$.
Clearly, $AB$ is the chord of contact of point $Q(\alpha, \beta)$ w.r.t. the ellipse (1). Therefore, equation of $AB$ will be $\frac{x\alpha}{a^2} + \frac{y\beta}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (2)
Since line (2) passes through $P(x_1, y_1)$, therefore, $\frac{x_1\alpha}{a^2} + \frac{y_1\beta}{b^2} = 1$
Hence, locus of $Q(\alpha, \beta)$ i.e. equation of the polar of point $P(x_1, y_1)$ is \[\frac{xx_1}{a^2} + \frac{yy_1}{b^2} = 1\tag{6.12} \]

d:orderedlist.d:listitem: If the polar of $P$ w.r.t. an ellipse passes through $Q$, then polar of $Q$ w.r.t. the same ellipse will pass through $P$
The point of intersection o faany two lines is the pole of the line joining the poles of the two lines.

d:sect2.d:title: Diameter of an Ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: The locus of the middle points of a system of parallel chords of an ellipse is called a diameter of the ellipse.
Let the ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Let $AB$ be one chord of a system of parallel chords of slope $m$.
Let $P(\alpha,\beta)$ be the middle point of chord $AB$, then equation of $AB$ is
$\Rightarrow \frac{x\alpha}{a^2} + \frac{y\beta}{b^2} = \frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} + \frac{\beta^2}{b^2}\ldots$ (2)
Slope of line (2), $m = -\frac{b^2\alpha}{a^2\beta}$
Thus, locus of $P$ i.e. equation the diameter is \[ y = -\frac{b^2}{a^2}x\tag{6.13} \]
Note: Diameter of an ellipse passes through its center. Thus, a diameter of an ellipse is its chord passing through the center.
Conjugate Diameters: Two diameters of an ellipse are said to be conjugate diameters if each bisects the chords parallel to the other.
Clearly, if slope of a pair of conjugate diameters be $m_1$ and $m_2$, then $m_1m_2 = -\frac{b^2}{a^2}$, provided $m_1$ and $m_2$ are defined.
Major and minor axes of an ellipse are also a pair of conjugate diameters.

d:sect2.d:title: Eccentric Angles of the Ends of a Pair of Conjugate Diameters Differ by a Right Angle
d:sect2.d:para: Let $POP'$ and $QOQ'$ be a pair of conjugate diameters.
Let the eccentric angles of $P$ and $Q$ be $\theta$ and $\phi$, then $P = (a\cos\theta, b\sin\theta)$ and $Q = (a\cos\phi, b\sin\phi)$.
Slope of $POP' = \frac{b}{a}\tan\theta$ and slope of $QOQ' = \frac{b}{a}\tan\phi$.
Since $POP'$ and $QOQ'$ are conjugate diameters, therefore, $-\frac{b^2}{a^2}\tan\theta\tan\phi = -\frac{b^2}{a^2}\Rightarrow \tan\theta\tan\phi = -1$
$\Rightarrow \cos\theta\cos\phi + \sin\theta\sin\phi = \cos(\theta - \phi) = 0 \Rightarrow \theta - \phi = \pm\frac{\pi}{2}$.
Thus, if eccentric angle of $P$ is $\theta$, then eccentric angles of $Q, P', Q'$ will be $\theta + \frac{\pi}{2}, \theta + \pi$ and $\theta + \frac{3\pi}{2}$ respectively.

d:sect2.d:title: Director Circle of an Ellipse
d:sect2.d:para: Locus of the point of intersection of mutually perpendicular tangents to an ellipse is a circle called director circle of the ellipse.
Let the ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Equation of any tangent to ellipse (1) is $y = mx + \sqrt{a^2m^2 + b^2}\ldots$ (2)
Equestion of a tangent to ellipse (1) perpendicular to line (2) is $my + x = \sqrt{a^2 + b^2m^2}\ldots$ (3)
In order to find the locus of the point of intersection of line (2) and (3), we need to eliminate $m$.
Squaring (2) and (3) and adding gives us $\left(1 + m^2\right)\left(x^2 + y^2\right) = \left(1 + m^2\right)\left(a^2 + b^2\right)$
which is the equation of the director circle of the ellipse (1).

d:sect2.d:title: Focal Distances
d:sect2.d:para: The focal distances of the point $P(x, y)$ on the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ are $a + ex$ and $a - ex$.
Since $P$ lies on the ellipse, therefore, $PS' = ePM' = e\frac{|ex + a|}{e} = |ex + a| = a + ex$
Again $PS + ePM = e\frac{|ex - a|}{e} = |ex - a| = a - ex[\because |ex| < a]$
Cleaerly, $PS + PS' = 2a$.

d:sect2.d:title: Four Normals on an Ellipse from a Point
d:sect2.d:para: Let the ellipse be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} + \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Let $P(\alpha, \beta)$ be a point in the $xy$-plane.
Equation of any normal to the ellipse is $ax\sec\theta - by\csc\theta = a^2 - b^2\ldots$ (2)
If line (2) passes through $P(\alpha, \beta)$, then
$a\alpha\sec\theta - b\beta\csc\theta = a^2 - b^2\ldots$ (3)
$\Rightarrow b\beta t^4 - 2\left(a^2 - b^2 + a\alpha\right)t^3 - 2\left(a^2 - b^2 - a\alpha\right)t - b\beta = 0$, where $t = \tan\frac{\theta}{2}$
The above equation will give $4$ values of $t$. Corresponding to these four values of $t$, we will get four points on the ellipse the normals to which will pass through $P(\alpha, \beta)$.
Hence, in general four normals can be drawn from any to an ellipse. These four points are called co-normal points.

Corollary: If $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ be the eccentric angles of four points on the ellipse such that the normals at these points are concurrent, then $\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta$ is an odd multiple of $\pi$.

Let the normals be concurrent at $P(\alpha, \beta)$, then from previous section the equation $\Rightarrow b\beta t^4 - 2\left(a^2 - b^2 + a\alpha\right)t^3 - 2\left(a^2 - b^2 - a\alpha\right)t - b\beta = 0$ will have four roots, which are $\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}, \tan\frac{\beta}{2}, \tan\frac{\gamma}{2}$ and $\tan\frac{\delta}{2}$.
From Vieta's relations $\displaystyle\sum\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}\tan\frac{\beta}{2} = 0$ and $\displaystyle\prod\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} = -1$
Thus, $1 - \displaystyle\sum\tan\frac{\alpha}{2}\tan\frac{\beta}{2} + \prod\tan\frac{\alpha}{2} = 0$
The denominator of above equation is $0$, and hence, $\alpha + \beta + \gamma + \delta$ is an odd multiple of $\pi$.

d:sect2.d:title: Definition
d:sect2.d:para: A hyperbola is the locus of the point which moves such that the ratio of its distance from a fixed point and a fixed straight line is a constant(greater than unity).
The fixed point is called the focus, the fixed line the directrix and the constant ratio the eccentricity of the hyperbola. Eccentricity is denoted by $e$.
In the given figure $S$ is the focus and $MM'$ the directrix. Let $P$ be any given point on the hyperbola then $\frac{PS}{PN} = e > 1$.
Equation of the hyperbola can be obtained if the coordinates of its focus, equation of its directrix and the eccentricity are known.

d:sect2.d:title: Standard Equation of the Hyperbola
d:sect2.d:para: We will find the standard equation of hyperbola as $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.
Let $S$ be the focus and $MM'$ the directrix of the hyperbola. Draw $SH\perp MM'$.
We divide $SH$ internally and externally in the ratio $e:1(e > 1)$ at points $A$ and $A'$ respectively, then
$\frac{AS}{AH} = e\ldots$ (1) and $\frac{A'S}{A'H} = e\ldots$ (2)
Clearly, $A$ and $A'$ will lie on the parabola. Let $AA' = 2a$. Let $O$ be the middle point of $AA'$. We take $O$ as the origin and $OS$ and $OY$ as $x$ and $y$ axes respectively.
From (1), $AS = eAH$ and from (3), $A'S = eA'H\Rightarrow A'S - AS = e\left(A'H - AH\right)$.

d:para.m: $\Rightarrow AA' = e\left(AA' - AH - AH\right) = e(2a - 2AH)\Rightarrow 2a = 2e(a - AH)\Rightarrow \frac{a}{e} = a - AH$

d:sect2.d:para: $\Rightarrow AH = a - \frac{a}{e}\ldots$ (3)
From (1), $AS = eAH = ae - a \therefore OS = OA + AS = a + ae - a = ae \therefore S = (ae, 0)\ldots$ (4)
Also $OH = OA - AH = a - \left(a - \frac{a}{e}\right) = \frac{a}{e}$
Therefore, equation of $MM'$ is $x = \frac{a}{e}$ or $ex - a = 0\ldots$ (5)
Let $P(\alpha, \beta)$ be a point on the hyperbola. We draw $PN\perp MM'$.
Then $\frac{PS}{PN} = e$ or $PS^2 = e^2PN^2\Rightarrow (\alpha - ae)^2 + \beta^2 = e^2\left(\frac{|e\alpha - a|}{e}\right)^2\ldots$ (6)
$\Rightarrow \frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} - \frac{\beta^2}{a^2\left(e^2 - 1\right)} = 1\Rightarrow \frac{\alpha^2}{a^2} - \frac{\beta^2}{b^2} = 1$, where $b^2 = (e^2 - 1)a^2$
Hence locus of $P(\alpha, \beta)$ i.e. equation of the hyperbola is \[\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\tag{6.15}\]

Note: From (6) it is clear than if focus of the hyperbola is $(-ae, 0)$ and directrix is $x = -\frac{a}{e}$, then also equation of the hyperbola will be same. Thus, hyperbola has two foci; $(ae, 0)$ and $(-ae, 0)$ with two directrices $x = \frac{a}{e}$ and $x = -\frac{a}{e}$.

d:sect2.d:title: Graph of a Hyperbola
d:sect2.d:para: Let the equation of the hyperbola is $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$(1)
The graph is given below:
(i) When $y = 0, x = \pm a$. Therefore, hyperbola cuts the $x$-axis at $(a, 0)$ and $(-a, 0)$
(ii) When $x = 0, y^2 = -b^2$, which is not possible. Hence, the hyperbola does not cut the $y$-axis.
(iii) When $y$ is replaced by $-y$, the equation of hyperbola does not change, hence it is symmetrical about $x$-axis.
(iv) When $x$ is replaced by $-x$, the equation of hyperbola does not change, hence it is symmetrical about $y$-axis.
(v) From (1), $y = \pm\frac{b}{a}\sqrt{x^2 - a^2}$. Since $y$ is real, therefore, $x^2 - a^2 \geq 0\Rightarrow x\leq -a$ or $x\geq a$.
Hence, no part of the parabola will lie between the lines $x = -a$ and $x = a$.
When $x\rightarrow \infty, y\rightarrow \pm\infty$ and when $x\rightarrow -\infty, y\rightarrow \pm\infty$
Also, $x = \pm\frac{a}{b}\sqrt{y^2 + b^2}$. Hence, $x$ is reall for all real values of $y$. Thus, $-\infty < y < \infty$

d:sect2.d:title: Terms Related to Hyperbola
d:sect2.d:para: Given below are some terms related to hyperbola.

d:figure.d:title: Conjugate axes and latus rectum of a hyperbola

d:orderedlist.d:listitem: Vertices and transverse axis: If the line perpendicular to the directrix from focus cuts the hyperbola at two points $A$ and $A'$, then $A$ and $A'$ are called the vertices and $AA'$ the transverse axis of the hyperbola.

Conjugate axis: The hyperbola does not meet at $y$-axis. However, we take two points $B_1$ and $B_2$ on $y$-axis, on opposite side of center $O$ of the hyperbola such that $OB_1 = OB_2 = b$. $B_1B_2$ is called the conjugate axis of the parabola.

d:listitem.d:para: Latus rectum: The chord of the hyperbola through its focus and perpendicular to the transverse axis is called the latus rectum.

d:sect2.d:title: An Important Property
d:sect2.d:para: The difference of the focal distances of any point on a hyperbola is a constant and is equal to the length of the transverse axis of the hyperbola.
Let $P(x, y)$ be any point on the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^1} = 1 \ldots$ (1)
Now $SP = ePN = eQM\ldots$ (2) and $S'P = ePN' = eMQ'\ldots$ (3)
Subtracting (2) from (3) gives us $S'P - SP = e(MQ' - QM)\ldots$ (4)
But $Q'M = QC + CM = \frac{a}{e} + x$ and $QM = CM - CQ = x - \frac{a}{e}$
Hence from (4), $S'P - SP = 2a = $ length of the transverse axis $A_1A_2$.

d:sect2.d:title: Conjugate Hyperbolas
d:sect2.d:para: The equation $\frac{y^2}{b^2} - \frac{x^2}{a^2} = 1$ is another standard form of equation of a hyperbola.
The transverse and conjugate axes of this hyperbola coincide with the conugate and transverse axes of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$.
Such hyperbolas are said to be conjugate to one another.

d:sect2.d:title: Tanngent to a Hyperbola
d:sect2.d:para: ELet the hyperbola be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Let $P = (x-1, y_1)$. From (1), $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{b^2}{a^2}\frac{x_1}{y_1}$ at $P$.
Equation of tangent at $P(x_1, y_1)$ is $y - y_1 = \frac{b^2}{a^2}\frac{x_1}{y_1}(x - x_1)$
which is the equation of a tangent to a parabola at $(x_1, y_1)$.
Thus, equation of tangent at $(a\sec\theta, b\tan\theta)$ is given by $\frac{x\sec\theta}{a} - \frac{y\tan\theta}{b} = 1$.

d:sect2.d:title: Normal to a Parabola
d:sect2.d:para: Let the hyperbola be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Let $P = (x-1, y_1)$. From (1), $\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{b^2}{a^2}\frac{x_1}{y_1}$ at $P$.
Equation of normal at $P(x_1, y_1)$ is $y - y_1 = -\frac{a^2}{b^2}\frac{y_1}{x_1}(x - x_1)$
which is the equation of a normal to a parabola at $(x_1, y_1)$.
Thus, equation of normal at $(a\sec\theta, b\tan\theta)$ is given by $ax\cos\theta + by\cot\theta = a^2 + b^2$.

d:sect2.d:title: Condition for a Line $y = mx + c$ to be a Tangent to a Hyperbola
d:sect2.d:para: Let the hyperbola be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Let given line be $y = mx + c\ldots$ (2)
Solving gives us $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{(mx + c)^2}{b^2} = 1$
$\Rightarrow \left(b^2 - a^2m^2\right)x^2 - 2a^2mcx - a^2\left(c^2 + b^2\right) = 0\ldots$ (3)
Line (2) will be tangent if roots of (3) are equal i.e. $D = 0$
\Rightarrow a^2m^2c^2 + b^2c^2 - a^2c^2m^2 + b^4 - a^2b^2m^2 = 0
which is the required condition.
Thus, we find two tangents $y = mx + \sqrt{a^2m^2 - b^2}$ and $y = mx - \sqrt{a^2m^2 - b^2}$.

d:sect2.d:title: Aymptote of a Hyperbola
d:sect2.d:para: An asymptote of a conic is a straight line which meets the curve in two points which are at infinity but which itself does not lie entirely at infinity. A hyperbola has two asymptotes.
Let the hyperbola be $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (1)
Let $P(x_1, y_1)$ be a point on hyperbola (1), then $\frac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \frac{y_1^1}{b^2} = 1\ldots$ (2)
Equation of tangent to hyperbola (1) at $P$ is $\frac{xx_1}{a^2} - \frac{yy_1}{b^2} = 1\ldots$(3)
$\Rightarrow \frac{x}{a^2}\mp\frac{y}{ab}\sqrt{1 - \frac{a^2}{x_1^2}} = \frac{1}{x_1}\ldots$ (4)
When $x_1\rightarrow\infty$, line (4) becomes $\frac{x}{a^2}\mp\frac{y}{ab}\Rightarrow \frac{x}{a} \mp \frac{y}{b} = 0$.
Thus, asymptotes of hyperbola (1) are $y = \pm\frac{b}{a}x\ldots$ (5)
Combined equation of asymptotes is $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 0\ldots$ (6)

d:sect2.d:title: Rectangular or Equilateral Hyperbola
d:sect2.d:para: For rectangular hyperbola $a = b$, therefore, equation of rectangular hyperbola is $x^2 - y^2 = a^2$.
We see that asymptotes are right angle each inclined to $x$-axis at an angle of $45^\circ$.
Rotating the axes through an angle of $45^\circ$ in clockwise direction makes the equation of rectangular hyperbola as
$\Rightarrow xy = \frac{a^2}{2} = c^2$, where $c^2 = \frac{a^2}{2}$.
Thus, equation of a rectangular hyperbola when its asymptotes are taken as axes is \[xy = c^2\tag{6.18}\]
Note: If we rotate the axes through the same aangle in anti-clockwise direction, then equation of rectangular hyperbola will be $xy = -\frac{a^2}{2}$.
If equation of a rectangular hyperbola is $xy = c^2$, then the equation of its conjugate hyperbola will be $xy = -c^2$.

d:sect2.d:title: Parametric Equation of a Rectangular Hyperbola
d:sect2.d:para: Parametric equation of the rectangular hyperbola $xy = c^2$ is $x = ct, y = \frac{c}{t}$.
Thus, coordinates of any points on the rectangular hyperbola $xy = c^2$ may be taken as $\left(ct, \frac{c}{t}\right)$.
The point $\left(ct, \frac{c}{t}\right)$ is also called the point '$t$'.

d:orderedlist.d:listitem: Equation of the chord of the hyperbola $xy = c^2$ joining points $t_1$ and $t_2$ is $x + t_1t_2y = c(t_1 + t-2)$.
The equation of the tangent to hyperbola $xy = c^2$ at '$t$' is $x + t^2y = 2ct$.
The equation of the normal to hyperbola $xy = c^2$ at '$t$' is $y - t^2x = \frac{c}{t}\left(1 - t^4\right)$ or $t^3x - ty - ct^4 + c = 0$.

d:sect2.d:title: Some Equations Related to Hyperbolas

d:orderedlist.d:listitem: Equation of the chord of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ whose middle point is $(x_1, y_1)$ is $T = S_1$ i.e. $\frac{xx_1}{a^2} - \frac{yy_1}{b^2} - 1 = \frac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \frac{y_1^2}{b^2} - 1$.
Point $(x_1, y_1)$ lies inside, in or outside the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ according as $\frac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \frac{y_1^2}{b^2} <, =$ or $> 1$.

Equation of pair of tangents from point $(x_1, y_1)$ to the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ is $SS_1 = T^2$ i.e. $\left(\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} - 1\right)\left(\frac{x_1^2}{a^2} - \frac{y_1^2}{b^2} - 1\right) = \left(\frac{xx_1}{a^2} - \frac{yy_1}{b^2} - 1\right)^2$
Equation of chord of contact of point $(x_1, y_1)$ w.r.t. the hyperbola is $T = 0$ or $\frac{xx_1}{a^2} - \frac{yy_1}{b^2} = 1$.

Equation of chord of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$ joining points $(a\sec\theta_1, b\tan\theta_1)$ and $(a\cos\theta_1, b\tan\theta_1)$ is $\frac{x}{x}\cos\left(\frac{\theta_1 - \theta_2}{2}\right) - \frac{y}{b}\sin\left(\frac{\theta_1 + \theta_2}{2}\right) = \cos\frac{\theta_1 + \theta_2}{2}$.

d:sect2.d:title: Diameter of a Conic
d:sect2.d:para: It is the locus of the middle points of a conic of all parallel chords. In order to find the equation of any diameter, slope of parallel chords must be known. The locus of the middle points of a system of parallel chords of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{a^1} = 1$ with slope $m$ is $y = \frac{b^2}{a^2m}x$.
Thus, the equation of the diameter of the hyperbola $\frac{x^2}{a^2} - \frac{y^2}{b^2} = 1$, which is the locus of middle points of parallel chords having slope $m$ is $y = \frac{b^2}{a^2m}x$.
